title: Nets & Spatial Visualization
coreInsight: A two-dimensional net can encode a three-dimensional solid's adjacency and orientation, and mental folding is a transformation problem.
targetLearnerRealization: A cube net records hinges rather than finished proximity; track each face through quarter-turns, preserve shared-edge adjacency, and use opposite pairs to reason without guessing.
learningObjectives: Interpret shared net edges as fold hinges.
Track face adjacency and orientation through quarter-turn folds.
Determine opposite cube faces from a valid net.
Recognize rotated copies as the same net arrangement.
Apply a fold-and-roll routine to unfamiliar valid cube nets.

continuity.openingCallback: Cut G10's exposed cube faces along selected edges and lay the connected skin flat without changing any face shape.
closingSeeds: Geometry is complete: angle, length, area, volume, transformation, and spatial structure can now be coordinated as one toolkit.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Squares that are close in a net must be adjacent after folding.
Opposite faces can be identified from flat distance alone.
Orientation is preserved without mental rotation.
Two rotated versions of the same net represent different solids.

beats.purpose: Make a labeled cube net the lesson medium and replace visual guessing with a traceable fold path.
beats.expectedRealization: The path G→Y→W can be followed as two hinge rotations, and the completed fold places B opposite W.
beats.transitionIn: G10 ended by cutting a solid's outer skin into a connected flat arrangement. Reverse that motion on this labeled skin.
beats.whyNow: The authentic problem exactly exposes the difference between flat position and three-dimensional relationship.
beats.entryBridge: Before choosing, highlight W and predict which way it rotates at each shared edge.
beats.exitBridge: The fold resolves opposite pairs W–B, G–O, and Y–R; therefore W is opposite B.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The exact labeled net and its foldable three-dimensional counterpart.
learnerPrompts: Which edge is the first hinge on the path toward W?
After crossing G→Y, which quarter-turn remains?
Which face arrives on the other side of W?
What are all three opposite pairs?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Trace G→Y→W as hinge rotations and keep top/bottom faces paired while the cube rolls.

steps.title: Trace hinges
steps.body: Move from G through Y to W; each shared edge is a quarter-turn hinge.

steps.title: Track opposites
steps.body: Completing the fold gives W–B, G–O, and Y–R as opposite pairs.

steps.title: Choose
steps.body: The face opposite W is B, so the answer is A.

resolution.takeaway: Fold along connected edges and track orientation; do not judge opposite faces by flat distance.

beats.purpose: Separate guaranteed net adjacency from accidental flat proximity.
beats.expectedRealization: A shared segment in the net is a hinge and guarantees cube-edge adjacency after folding; mere closeness does not.
beats.transitionIn: The animation followed a path only across edges the squares actually share.
beats.prompt: Which flat relationship is guaranteed to survive when a valid net folds?

options.text: Two faces sharing a full net edge remain adjacent along that cube edge.
Two faces touching only at a flat corner become opposite.
The two visually closest labels become adjacent.
Every pair in the same flat row remains coplanar.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. A shared edge is a physical hinge joining the same two faces.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Imagine tape along each uncut segment: that segment stays joined while the faces rotate around it.

steps.body: Folding changes angles between faces, not which two faces own an uncut shared edge. Flat distance without a shared edge gives no such guarantee.

beats.purpose: Find an opposite face by surrounding a chosen base with its four neighbors.
beats.expectedRealization: A cube face has four adjacent faces and exactly one opposite face.
beats.transitionIn: Once hinge adjacencies are recorded, use the cube's six-face structure to finish relationships that were not connected in the net.
beats.prompt: In a net, face Q folds with P, R, T, and U around its four edges. The only remaining face is S. What is S relative to Q?

options.text: Opposite Q
The same face as Q
Hinged directly to Q in the net
Impossible to determine

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Four faces fill Q's four adjacent positions, leaving S opposite Q.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A cube face has four edge-neighbors and one opposite among the other five faces.

steps.body: List Q's four adjacent faces first. The sixth face cannot share an edge with Q, so it must be opposite.

resolution.takeaway: Four neighbors plus one leftover identifies an opposite pair.

beats.purpose: Make orientation change explicit under a hinge rotation.
beats.expectedRealization: A face rotates rigidly about its shared edge, so markings rotate with the face rather than staying fixed on the page.
beats.transitionIn: Knowing which face lands somewhere is not enough when arrows, dots, or labels have direction.
beats.prompt: A marked square folds upward 90° about its bottom edge. What happens to an arrow drawn on that square?

options.text: It rigidly rides with the face through the same 90° rotation.
It stays in its original page direction while the face turns.
It reflects across the hinge.
Its direction becomes undefined.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The marking and face undergo one rigid rotation together.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Treat the face as a stiff card: ink cannot remain behind while the card turns.

steps.body: The hinge fixes one edge. Every other point on the face travels on a quarter-circle, preserving distances, angles, and the marking's orientation relative to that face.

resolution.takeaway: Rotate the marking with its face at every hinge.

beats.purpose: Treat a planar rotation of an entire net as a representation change, not a new solid.
beats.expectedRealization: Rotating or reflecting the whole paper preserves its square adjacency graph and foldability.
beats.transitionIn: G9 distinguished a moved copy from a changed shape. Apply that invariant to the entire flat net.
beats.prompt: A valid cube net is turned 90° on the table without moving any square relative to another. What changes?

options.text: Only its page orientation; it folds to the same cube.
Its opposite-face pairs change.
It becomes invalid.
Its shared-edge hinges disappear.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. A whole-net rotation preserves every connection and fold instruction.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Rotate the paper as one rigid object; its adjacency graph is unchanged.

steps.body: Translation, rotation, or reflection of the complete diagram changes how we view it but preserves which squares share edges.

resolution.takeaway: Compare net structure up to rigid motion of the page.

beats.purpose: Name a reusable spatial reasoning routine after the learner has used its components.
beats.expectedRealization: A net is an adjacency-and-orientation encoding reconstructed through hinge rotations.
beats.name: Fold tracking
beats.conciseDefinition: A net is a connected flat arrangement of a solid's faces. Shared edges act as hinges; folding rotates faces into space while preserving each face's shape and markings.
beats.formalization: shared edge → adjacent faces · four neighbors + one leftover → opposite · marking follows every hinge rotation
beats.memoryHook: Hinge, rotate, record; never guess by flat distance.

beats.purpose: Assess opposite-face elimination in a standard cross net.
beats.whyNow: Begin independent work with one face having four visible hinge neighbors.
beats.entryBridge: List B's four edge-neighbors before looking at the remaining square.
beats.exitBridge: A, C, E, and F surround B, leaving D opposite B.
learnerPrompts: Which four faces already occupy B's adjacent positions?
beats.incorrectFeedback: B shares net edges with A, C, E, and F; the sixth face is opposite.

steps.body: The four faces hinged directly to B become its four cube neighbors. D is the only remaining face, so B–D is an opposite pair.

resolution.takeaway: The leftover-face method works when four neighbors are visible.

beats.purpose: Assess hinge-path tracking on a differently oriented valid net.
beats.entryBridge: Fold outward from B and record which faces fill opposite directions.
beats.exitBridge: The valid T-net resolves D opposite F.
learnerPrompts: Which face swings across D's opposite direction?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use B as a starting face: D and F fold from opposite edges of B.

steps.body: D is above B and F is below B. Their hinge rotations place them on opposite cube faces.

resolution.takeaway: Faces attached to opposite edges of one face become opposite.

beats.purpose: Assess all three pairs rather than one target face.
beats.whyNow: Coordinate the full six-face structure of the T-net.
beats.entryBridge: Each found pair removes two faces from consideration.
beats.exitBridge: The three pairs are A–C, B–E, and D–F.
learnerPrompts: After finding one pair, which four faces remain?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Those three disjoint pairs account for every face.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Track the left/right, central/extended, and above/below directions separately.

steps.body: A and C fold from opposite sides; D and F fold from opposite sides; the extended E closes opposite B.

resolution.takeaway: A cube's six faces partition into exactly three opposite pairs.

beats.purpose: Assess adjacency created by folding between faces not hinged together in the flat net.
beats.whyNow: Directly confront the belief that only flat neighbors can become cube neighbors.
beats.entryBridge: On a cube, distinct faces are adjacent unless they form an opposite pair.
beats.exitBridge: A and E do not share a net edge but are adjacent after folding; the other listed pairs are opposite.
learnerPrompts: Which options are known opposite pairs?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. A and E meet along a cube edge after folding.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Eliminate A–C, B–D, and E–F because they are opposite pairs.

steps.body: The cross net gives opposites A–C, B–D, and E–F. Therefore A and E are non-opposite distinct faces and must share a cube edge.

resolution.takeaway: Folding creates cube adjacencies beyond the hinges drawn in the net.

beats.purpose: Assess orientation across a sequence of spatial rotations.
beats.whyNow: Finish independent work by composing folds with two cube rolls.
beats.entryBridge: Write the top, bottom, north, south, east, and west faces, then update one roll at a time.
beats.exitBridge: Rolling right brings A to top; rolling away next brings F to top.
learnerPrompts: Which face becomes top after only the first roll?
Which side then moves to top on the second roll?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The final top face is F.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Start with B top, A west, C east, E away, F toward you, and D bottom; update one roll at a time.

steps.title: Roll right
steps.body: The west face A rises to the top.

steps.title: Roll away
steps.body: The toward-you face F rises to the top, so the final answer is F.

resolution.takeaway: Compose spatial rotations one step at a time and carry the full orientation state forward.

beats.purpose: Assess an unfamiliar net with no four-armed center.
beats.whyNow: Use the hinge routine on a turning six-square chain where flat distance is especially misleading.
beats.entryBridge: Follow the staircase A→B→C→D→E→F and rotate at every turn.
beats.exitBridge: The resulting opposite pairs are A–D, B–E, and C–F, so F is opposite C.
learnerPrompts: How does each right-angle turn change the next face's spatial direction?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Track face normals through the path's alternating up and right hinge turns.

steps.body: Assign A as a reference face and fold successively north, east, north, east, north. The normals pair as A–D, B–E, and C–F.

resolution.takeaway: A stepwise orientation record works even when the net has no obvious center.

beats.expectedRealization: Hinges, orientation states, adjacency, and opposite-pair checks provide independent evidence.
beats.transitionIn: The cross, T, and staircase nets looked different, but the same fold records solved all of them.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable net-folding routine? Select all four.

options.text: Mark full shared edges as hinges.
Rotate each face and its markings together.
Record adjacent and opposite relationships as they become fixed.
Treat whole-paper rotations as the same net structure.

response.feedback: Together these actions replace flat-picture intuition with invariant tracking.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Track the hinge motion and relationships while ignoring irrelevant page orientation.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four are needed for a stable spatial record.

steps.body: Shared edges supply the rotations; orientation records determine placement; the cube's four-neighbor/one-opposite structure checks the result.

beats.purpose: Close the geometry strand by connecting flat and spatial invariants.
beats.expectedRealization: Spatial visualization coordinates earlier geometry ideas rather than replacing them.
beats.transitionIn: A net preserves face shapes from G10 and moves them by G9's rigid rotations until three-dimensional adjacency emerges.
beats.prompt: When a flat net becomes a cube, which quantities and relationships stay fixed, and which ones change because the faces rotate into space?
beats.takeaway: Geometry becomes dependable when every transformation is paired with an explicit invariant and a record of what changes.

notes: Design: the approved bank problem opens the lesson and its five-step cube-net animation becomes the discovery medium. Learners then extract hinge, orientation, opposite-pair, and whole-net equivalence tools before independent transfer.
Beat outline: authentic W-face prediction -> hinge invariant -> opposite elimination -> orientation -> paper rotation -> name -> six independent items -> consolidation -> geometry synthesis.
The mapped CubeNetOppositeFaceScene is referenced unchanged with lesson-controlled playback across its full timeline; no animation or renderer source was modified.

Generated results were checked using independent face-normal propagation, four-neighbor elimination, opposite-pair inventories, and stepwise cube orientation updates. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
